client: I've been really anxious about this weekend because my partner wants me to meet their friends for the first time, and I just can't stop thinking about it. I keep imagining them judging me or thinking I'm not good enough for my partner. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to make the anxiety go away — it feels too real and too close.
therapist: It makes a lot of sense that this feels so real and pressing — anticipating judgment from people who matter to your partner is genuinely unsettling, and that worry can feel very hard to shake. I also hear your skepticism about whether talking will even help, and I want to honor that; sometimes the anxiety feels bigger than any conversation. Can you tell me a little more about what specifically you imagine these friends thinking or saying about you — what does that inner critic's voice sound like?

client: Honestly, the voice in my head is pretty brutal — it's like I can already hear them whispering that I'm not good enough for my partner, that I'm too anxious or awkward or just... not the kind of person they'd want around. It's almost like I'm writing the script for them before I even walk in the room. And the worst part is, I can't tell if I actually believe those things about myself or if I'm just terrified they will.
therapist: That image of "writing the script for them" is really insightful — you're essentially handing your inner critic a megaphone and letting it narrate a story that hasn't even happened yet, which sounds exhausting and painful. What strikes me is that important question you're sitting with: whether these harsh judgments feel true about *you*, or whether they're fears you're projecting outward — that distinction is actually really worth exploring. When you hear that voice say "I'm too awkward or not good enough," what evidence do you find yourself reaching for, either to challenge it or to confirm it?

client: Honestly, when I hear that voice, I almost always reach for the confirming evidence first — like, I'll immediately think of that time at my coworker's birthday thing where I stood in the corner and nobody really came to talk to me for most of the night. That feels like proof, you know? And I know I should probably look for the other side, but the challenging evidence feels so much flimsier, like I'm just making excuses for myself.
therapist: It's really common for our minds to treat painful memories like solid proof while dismissing the positive ones as "just excuses" — but that asymmetry itself is worth noticing, because it tells us something about how your inner critic operates, not necessarily about reality. That night at the birthday party sounds lonely, but I'm curious — is it possible there were other explanations for what happened there, ones that had nothing to do with your worth as a person? And when you try to reach for the challenging evidence, what's one moment, even a small one, where you genuinely connected with someone or felt accepted?

client: I mean... yeah, maybe some people at that party were just distracted or had their own stuff going on. But it's hard not to take it personally when you're standing there and nobody's really making an effort to include you. As for a moment where I felt connected... there was this one time a few months ago when a coworker and I stayed late working on a project and we just ended up talking for like an hour about nothing important, and it actually felt really easy and natural. But then I think, okay, that was just one time, and we haven't really talked much since, so maybe it didn't mean as much to them as it did to me.
therapist: That memory of the easy, natural conversation is actually really meaningful — and I notice your mind immediately moved to minimize it, turning "this felt good" into "but maybe it didn't count." That's your inner critic doing exactly what it does best: moving the goalposts so no positive evidence ever quite qualifies. I'm wondering if we can sit with that moment a little longer — not as proof that you're universally likeable, but just as genuine data that ease and connection *are* possible for you. What do you think was different about you in that conversation compared to how you imagine yourself this weekend?

client: I guess... when I was talking to Marcus, I wasn't really thinking about how I was coming across. I was just actually interested in what he was saying about his trip, so I forgot to monitor myself the whole time. But I don't know if that's something I can just switch on this weekend — it's not like I can force myself to stop being self-conscious around people I barely know.
therapist: What you just described is actually a really important insight — when you were genuinely curious about Marcus, the self-monitoring quietly stepped aside on its own, which suggests it's not about willpower or "switching something on," but about where your attention is directed. You're right that you can't force it, but you also don't have to — curiosity tends to be a more natural path in than trying to silence the self-conscious voice directly. So I'm wondering: is there anything you're genuinely curious about your partner's friends, even something small, that you could hold onto as a kind of anchor going into this weekend?

client: I mean... yeah, I guess I am kind of curious about what Jamie does for work, because Marcus mentioned something about her switching careers and I never really got the full story. But I'm worried that even if I start out curious, the moment there's a lull in conversation or someone looks at me a certain way, I'll just spiral back into my head and lose it. It feels fragile, like curiosity is this tiny flame that anxiety can just snuff out really easily.
therapist: That image of curiosity as a tiny flame is really beautiful and honest — and I think you're right that anxiety can feel like a strong wind, but flames also have a way of rekindling, especially when you have something real to return to, like genuinely wanting to hear Jamie's story. The lulls and the looks that might pull you back into your head are real risks, but they don't have to mean the night is lost — they can just be moments where you gently redirect back to that curiosity, even imperfectly. What do you think it would feel like to give yourself permission to spiral a little and still come back, rather than needing to hold it all together perfectly?

client: Honestly, that idea of giving myself permission to spiral a little... it both appeals to me and terrifies me at the same time. Like, part of me thinks if I let myself start to slip, I won't be able to pull back, and then I'll just ruin the whole evening for both of us. I guess I don't fully trust that I have that ability to redirect myself once the anxiety really kicks in.
therapist: That fear of a spiral becoming a freefall makes a lot of sense, and it's worth taking seriously — but I'd gently point out that you've actually already demonstrated that redirection ability today, right here in this conversation. You moved from "talking won't help" to uncovering a real insight about curiosity and self-monitoring, and each time your inner critic minimized something, a part of you was able to step back and look at it differently. What do you think that part of you — the one that can observe the critic and question it — would need to feel even a little more trustworthy to you going into this weekend?

client: That's... actually kind of hard to dismiss, when you put it that way. I did notice myself shifting a little, even though part of me kept wanting to shut it down. I think for that observing part to feel more trustworthy, it would need to not feel so exhausting — like, right now it takes so much effort to step back from the critic that I'm not sure I'd have the energy to do it when I'm alone and the anxiety is louder.
therapist: It's really significant that you noticed that shift happening, even against resistance — that's not nothing, that's actually evidence of a skill that exists in you, even if it's still effortful and tiring. The exhaustion makes complete sense, because right now that observing part is working against a very loud, well-practiced critic, and that's like swimming upstream; over time, with practice, it does tend to get lighter. I'm curious — when you imagine being alone this weekend before you head out, what do you think would help that observing part feel even slightly more resourced, whether that's something you do, something you remind yourself of, or even just how you talk to yourself in that moment?

client: I guess... maybe reminding myself that the loneliness I feel before going out isn't proof that something is wrong with me, or that I'll always feel that way. But honestly, even saying that out loud, there's a part of me that's already rolling its eyes at it, like it sounds too neat, too much like a affirmation poster. I don't know if I actually believe it in the moment, even if I can say it right now.
therapist: That eye-roll is actually really valuable information — it's telling you that your mind needs something that feels *earned* and specific, not generic, and that's a healthy kind of skepticism. So instead of a broad affirmation, what if the reminder was rooted in something concrete you discovered today — something like "I connected easily with Marcus when I was curious, and I'm curious about Jamie's story," which is true and particular to you, not something off a poster. Does that feel any different to sit with, or does the skeptical part still want to push back on that too?

client: Okay, that one actually lands a little differently, I'll admit it. It's specific enough that I can't just dismiss it the way I would "you're worthy of connection" or whatever. But I guess my worry is that even if I carry that thought with me to Jamie's party, the moment I walk in and feel that wave of anxiety, it's going to get drowned out by everything else going on in my head.
therapist: It's really encouraging that something finally landed — and that specificity is exactly what makes it stickable. The wave of anxiety when you walk in is real and likely *will* happen, but the thought doesn't need to compete with it in that moment; it just needs to be something you can return to after the wave peaks, the way you described coming back to curiosity with Marcus. What if you thought of it less like a shield to keep the anxiety out, and more like a small anchor you know is there when you're ready to reach for it — does that feel like a more workable way to carry it in?
